## Sentences of the specification made false

- `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5486-5488`, in the effect of Appendix I's entry "The numeral types, their conversion and their default" (`\subsection` at `:5161`, `\item[Effect]` at `:5374`). Before: "The implementations depart from the text in these further ways, each with its row of the revival's gap ledger: a numeral with a radix point keeps only one of its leading zeros in its digit count, as the parser gives the numeral to both implementations (row~960); the interpreter loads and runs a program that writes a numeral type in a \KWD{comprises} clause (row~981); ...". After (`:5485-5487`): "The implementations depart from the text in these further ways, each with its row of the revival's gap ledger: the interpreter loads and runs a program that writes a numeral type in a \KWD{comprises} clause (row~981); ...", the sentence's other clauses whole. Edited in `535ad0a5c7`.
- `grep -rn '~960' Specification --include=*.tex` on the base printed one line, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5488`, the clause above, which the change made false and which is removed; on the final tree it prints nothing.
- `grep -rn -i 'leading zero' Specification --include=*.tex` prints four other lines, each true now: `basic/expressions/literals.tex:101` (the rule), `:151` (the Working Draft's `Literal`, in a `\revision`), `basic/expressions/constant.tex:147` (a concatenation of natural numerals counts its leading zeros), and `appendices/changes.tex:5510` (original text quoted). No `\note` or `\revision` box names the parser's trim.
- Outside the specification, for the gather: the skill's `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/interpreter.md:26`, "A numeral with a radix point keeps only one of its leading zeros, so a coercion over `RadixPointNumeral[\n, m, r, v\]` gets `n` = 2 for `00.5`, not 3 (ledger row 960).", is false now; and P-174's last sentence, "Rows 960 and 981 hold where the tree departs: the digit count of `00.5`, and walk running a numeral type written in a `comprises` clause." (`explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md:106`), holds for row 981 only.

## The two stages, on the final tree

Every path the rung changes outside the exempt folders is `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nodes_util/ExprFactory.java`, so both stages ran, once each, on `535ad0a5c7` (the code of `704d6fe747`), after the last edit was built; no code changed after them. The comparands are the last landed gate's tables, `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-34b/gate/checker-count.txt` and `distance.txt` (landed in `295c215c2c`), and `explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv`.

- The count, `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh tmp/rung-radix-point-leading-zeros/checker-count-postedit.txt tmp/rung-radix-point-leading-zeros/cc-post`: '#total 0', '#locations 0', '#crash none', '#shadow matches the tracked StaticChecker'; `diff explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-34b/gate/checker-count.txt tmp/rung-radix-point-leading-zeros/checker-count-postedit.txt` prints nothing (rc=0): the tables are the same, every api 0.
- The distance, `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh tmp/rung-radix-point-leading-zeros/distance-postedit.txt tmp/rung-radix-point-leading-zeros/dist-post`: '#total 0', every kind 0, '#crash none', '#seconds 117 FortressLibrary 74'. `explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/compare.sh explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-34b/gate/distance.txt tmp/rung-radix-point-leading-zeros/distance-postedit.txt` prints 'DISTANCE SAME   0'. `dist-post/errors.tsv` holds only its header, as does the per-site list: no site moved.

The edit changes no Scala of the checker and nothing the build generates for it, so compiler.md's "The checker's time" does not apply.

## The ladder subset

No file's recorded first error in the baseline (`explorations/compile-ladder/baseline-2026-09-19/raw/`, and its `ladder.tsv` for the files outside the pass list) names what the change touched: `grep -rl -i 'FloatLiteral\|makeFloatLiteralExpr\|ExprFactory\|leading zero\|RadixPointNumeral\|digit'` over `raw/` prints nothing. So the subset by the rule is empty. The two ladder files whose rows name a numeral or a float literal type ran instead, after the edit only, with the drivers copied to `tmp/rung-radix-point-leading-zeros/ladder/` as gate.md, "The ladder regression", says (`run-subset.sh`, then `classify.py`): 'sanity ok: library_tests/Integer1 compiles and prints PASS'; `tests/NumeralTest.fss` 'disambiguate', first error 'ImmutableArray is undefined.', as in the baseline's `ladder.tsv`; `tests/XXXextendFloatLiteral.fss` 'typecheck', as in the baseline, its first error now 'Type requires static arguments: CompilerBuiltin.RadixPointNumeral' where the baseline has the deleted trait `FloatLiteral`'s, since `3de571bac7` respelled the file's `extends`. Neither is in the gate's 85, so the newest landed `ladder.tsv` (`climb-batch-34b/gate/ladder/ladder.tsv`) holds neither. No move.

## Points to report

- The fix as made, and every reader of the node's text that now sees the leading zeros: `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nodes_util/ExprFactory.java:1637-1640`; the readers above ("Every reader of the node's text"), of which `NumeralNumbers.java:78`, `CoercionOracle.scala:223`, `:229`, `:621`, `IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java:257`, `:403` and `FortressAstToConcrete.java:1650` now see the zeros.
- Row 960's test promoted and its compiled twin, each failing on the base and passing after: `ProjectFortress/tests/RadixPointLeadingZerosWalk.fss:12`, `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/RadixPointLeadingZerosCompiled.fss:12`; the runs above.
- Each sentence of the specification that the change makes false, before and after: `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:5485-5487`, quoted above.
- The two stages' tables on the final tree against the comparand: the count's diff empty, the distance 'DISTANCE SAME   0', above.

Not reached: a file edited beyond those named (none: `git diff --name-only 13f4fdea75` lists `ExprFactory.java`, `changes.tex`, the four test files and this folder's two files); a pinned message or a test's checked value that changes (no test pins a message or checks a value with two leading zeros, by the greps above; the changed messages are unpinned); a model line (none changes). No step taken cannot be undone or acts against a decision on record.

## Decisions

1. **The node keeps the digits as written: the four lines of the trim deleted** (fork R1, the batch's default). Ways not taken: a separate count kept beside a trimmed text (R1's way not taken; it adds a field to `FloatLiteralExpr` in `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and regenerates the nodes, the checker's Scala face among them); `NumeralNumbers` counting from the source span (it would read the file again, and a generated or folded node has no span of its own digits); parsing the value from a trimmed copy and keeping the untrimmed text (two strings for one result: `new BigInteger` reads leading zeros, so the values are the same, as the `RR64` probe shows); an edit of `Literal.rats` (outside the rung's files, and its actions already pass the whole text, `Literal.rats:53-83`). Evidence: the precedent `ExprFactory.java:609-632`; P-174; `literals.tex:101`.
2. **The compiled twin in the promoted run-pair form**: `Name.fss`, `NameLink.test` with `link`, `Name.test` with `link`, `run` and `run_out_contains=PASS`, as `compiler_tests/NatRtTask.test` and `NatRtTaskLink.test` (tests-writing.md, "Promoting an `XXX` test"); the probe's second assertion, 2 digits for `0.5`, kept as the probe has it, so that the test also fails if `n` stops counting at all. Ways not taken: the probe's single `.test` with `link` and `run`; the twin asserting `00.5` only, as the walk test does. Evidence: the brief, "with its link test".
3. **Appendix I: the clause removed, the sentence's other clauses whole**, as the brief says. Way not taken: rewording the sentence's opening. Evidence: `changes.tex:5485-5487`.
4. **The ladder subset: the two near files run, though the rule's subset is empty.** Ways not taken: running nothing (the rule's literal answer), running the gate's 85 (the gate's work). Evidence: the greps of "The ladder subset".
5. **The two unit-test classes that call the factory run by `ant testOnly`** beside the brief's two suites, since the misc track is in neither. Way not taken: leaving them to the gate. Evidence: `NumeralFoldJUTest.java:29`, `ConstructorsJUTest.java:150-174`.
6. **The fold's `result` left as it is**: a folded `MIN`, `MAX` or `|x|` that answers a written radix-point operand keeps that operand's text, now with its zeros, while an integer operand is rewritten to its value's digits (`IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java:251-258`). Ways not taken: rewriting the kept text to the value's digits (`written`'s form) in this rung, a file beyond those named. Evidence: only a checker message shows it (the `MAX` probe), and no coercion reads a folded constant's numbers (P-174); put to the curator below.

## Questions for the curator

- Should a folded constant that keeps a written radix-point operand, as `00.5 MAX 0.1`, show the operand's digits in its numeral type (now `RadixPointNumeral[\3,1,10,5\]` in the checker's message), or its value's, as an integer operand kept so does (`IntegerLiteralFoldingVisitor.java:251-253`) and as `00.5 + 0.0` does (`[\2,1,10,5\]`)? Default: as it is; no program reads it (P-174), only the message shows it.

## Defects and their homes

- Row 960, the digit count of a numeral with a radix point: home 1, repaired, asserted by `ProjectFortress/tests/RadixPointLeadingZerosWalk.fss` (walk) and `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/RadixPointLeadingZerosCompiled.test` (compiled). The row closes.
- No other defect was measured. The folded `MAX`'s type in a message is no defect by any source: the specification gives a folded constant no numeral type of its own numbers, only its default and its conversion at the number types (`literals.tex`, the paragraph on static expressions), so it is the question above, without a row. The compiled probe's second error, 'ZZ has no getter called asZZ32', is the prelude's known limit until the switch-over (revival-changes.md, "Numbers", the low-bits paragraph; row 349); the twin uses the helper for it.

## For FACTS

content.content:
# Running tests

**track**
: One of the five JVMs of `ant testFast`.

**shard**
: One of the four JVMs of `ant testSystem`. Shard i of n takes every n-th file of the sorted list, from index i.

**code state**
: Code of a tree as one edit leaves it. Only an edit of code makes a new code state; a commit does not.

## The two suites

`ant testFast` runs its tests in five tracks, four at once, in about 11 minutes:

- compiler: `CompilerJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` and `parser_tests/`. It is the longest track, so it sets the total time.
- library: `LibraryJUTest` over `library_tests/`.
- othercompiler: `OtherCompilerJUTest` over `other_compiler_tests/`.
- misc: the unit `*JUTest` classes, except `OneLibraryJUTest`.
- onelibrary: `OneLibraryJUTest` over `one_library_tests/`, with `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. It starts when another track ends.

`ant testSystem` runs `SystemJUTest` over `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's test folder. It runs its tests in four shards, in a few minutes.

`ant testSpecData` runs the specification's 130 extracted examples (`SpecData/examples/basic`, `preliminaries`, `advanced`) under walk, in about a minute. The gate runs it after the two suites.

The newest gate summary has the exact counts and times of the last landed run:

    git log -1 --name-only --format= -- 'explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/gate/summary.txt'

The two suites work in the same way:

- Each suite runs `ant compileAll` first, as every `ant` test target does, so it never tests stale classes. After an edit of Java or Scala, that build empties `default_repository/caches` (`build-and-caches.md`, "Building"). Each analyses or compiles the Fortress code that it tests, in private caches.
- Each JVM gets 768 MB, a 32 MB stack and `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, whatever the shell exports. The run steps of the compiled tests get `JAVA_FLAGS=-Xmx4g -Xss64m`, also whatever the shell exports.
- Each suite deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when it starts. Each JVM keeps its caches in a folder of its own under it, so that the JVMs do not overwrite each other's entries. Temporary files go to `ProjectFortress/test-tmp/`.
- The results are in `ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`, as `TEST-<class>.txt`.

To run a suite:

- Run one suite at a time in a tree, because each suite deletes the `test-caches` that the other uses.
- Read the verdict in the line before `Total time:`: `BUILD SUCCESSFUL` means zero failures, and `BUILD FAILED` means at least one. Every `ant` test target ends with these lines, and exits non-zero when it failed.
- To compare test counts, compare the sum of the four shards. A file added to `tests/` moves every later file to another shard.
- If a suite's count fell, a `.test` file or a `tests=` line almost always went missing.

## The switches that the harness reads

Put a `-D` switch on the `java` line of a run by hand; the `java` line in `harness-one.sh` is a model. On the `ant` line, it does not reach the suites' JVMs.

- `-Dtests=<dir>`: the folder that `SystemJUTest` runs, in place of `tests/`.
- `-Dfortress.suite.shard=i/n`: run shard i of n only.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.count=N`: run N files at most.
- `-Dfortress.unittests.seed=<value>`: the order of the files. Each run prints its seed as `FORTRESS_UNITTESTS_SEED=...`.
- `FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1` for `SystemJUTest`, `-Dfortress.junit.verbose=true` for the compiled tests' classes: show the output of passing tests too.
- `-Dfortress.junit.reset=false`: `CompilerJUTest` and `LibraryJUTest` keep their caches folder. Without it, they empty it when they start.

## Outside the gate

- `ant testNotPassing` runs the interpreter programs of `ProjectFortress/not_passing_yet/`, which are expected to fail. It fails if one of them passes.
- No suite and no stage of the gate runs the team demos, the programs of `ProjectFortress/demos/`. Keep each of the 52 demos that `DemoTests` lists reaching its end (P-79). Check them with the demo driver below, not with `ant testDemos`, whose test of the output is weaker:
  - If your change edits walk, the parser, a phase that both paths run, a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`interpreter.md`, "Natives") or the interpreter's library, run the driver once, after your last edit of code.
  - Print the driver with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-team-demos/REPORT.md#Commands worked out'`. Save the first script that it prints, under "The demo driver", without the text around it, as `tmp/run-demos.sh` in your tree.
  - From the tree's root, after you set up the call, run `bash tmp/run-demos.sh tmp/demos`. It runs long, so run it in the background with a log (`session.md`, "Long commands"). It runs the demos under walk one at a time and writes `tmp/demos/summary.tsv`.
  - The driver's last line of output, before the log's `EXIT=` line, must read 'demos: 52 run, 52 reached their end'. A demo reaches its end if it exits 0 and its output holds no "fail" in upper or lower case.
  - If your change breaks a demo and you know how to repair the demo, repair it in the commit of your change. Otherwise, report the demo, its output and the ledger row that holds the missing feature, as a defect that your change makes or uncovers.
- Nothing runs these folders: `not_working_compiler_tests/`, `not_working_library_tests/`, `not_working_static_tests/`, `obsolete_interpreter_tests/`, `long_term_not_working/`, `linker_tests/`, `compiler_regressions/`. Put every new test in a gated test folder. A test of a defect that fails today is an `XXX` test there (`tests-writing.md`).

## When to run a whole suite

- The gate runs every suite once, on the tree that lands (`gate.md`). Your brief says whether you run the gate.
- If your edit changes the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk, of a phase that both paths share or of such a class under `nativeHelpers/`, run all the tests that it reaches. Run them once, after your last edit of code. The run needs no commit.
  - For the checker, run `ant testQuick`: the compiler, othercompiler and library tracks at once (below).
  - For walk, run `ant testSystem`. It is the same as its four shards run by hand.
  - For a shared phase (under `compiler/`: name binding, DSL grammars, desugaring, the marking of overloaded calls in `OverloadRewriter`), the parser or such a class, run both.
- Quote the verdict lines and the command in your report, with the commit if your code is committed.
- If the gate later runs on a tree that holds other changes too, that tree is another code state. Your run and the gate's run do not repeat each other.
- After an edit of the code generator (`codegen/`, `OverloadSet`) or the runtime (`runtimeSystem/`), run your own tests, and the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`) if `compiler.md` asks for them. Leave the whole tracks to the gate.
- After every other change, run only your own tests, through the scripts below, and the demos where "Outside the gate" asks for them. Leave the rest to the gate. This includes an edit of either library, though it reaches many tests. After an edit of one of the fourteen components that `OneLibraryComponents.test` compiles, also run `ant testOneLibrary` (`library.md`, "Designing a change").

The suites do not check these:

- the bytecode optimizer, which nothing in the compiler calls;
- DSL grammars, except one program whose phases the misc track runs: `syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss`;
- the linker's aliasing of apis;
- `fortress unparse`;
- the round trip of the `.tfi` and `.tfs` caches;
- a behaviour above one thread that one run of each suite at four threads does not hit.

If your edit is in one of these, your own tests are its only check. Say so in your report.

## One test, or a few

Each script and `fortress junit` below ends with the verdict of JUnit's text runner: `OK (n tests)`, or `FAILURES!!!` with the counts. Read the verdict there: the exit code is 0 whatever the verdict.

### Interpreter tests

Run interpreter tests (`ProjectFortress/tests/`) from the tree's root, after you set up the call:

    explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh <tree>/tmp/h1 \
        ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss [ProjectFortress/tests/X.test] [more files ...]

- It runs `SystemJUTest` with testSystem's JVM settings, at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`, on a folder that holds only the files that you name.
- It keeps its cache in the folder `<scratch-dir>.cache`. It starts from that cache while the build and the library sources are those that filled it. Otherwise, or with `COLD_CACHE=1`, it starts empty. Its first line says `cache filled` or `cache empty`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing. After you edit Java, Scala or a parser grammar, run `ant compileAll` first. If your tree has no build, seed it or build it as `worktrees.md` says.
- Give it a scratch directory that holds nothing else. The script deletes the directory when it starts and when it ends.
- If a test has an `X.test` file (its keys for a refusal at load), name it beside its `X.fss`.
- It takes 15 to 25 s with an empty cache, mostly to analyse the library, and about 4 s with a filled one. Name several files in one call to run them in one JVM.
- It shows the output of passing tests too, and removes the Java stack frames.

To see the whole diagnostic, with its Java stack, run the program directly, from `ProjectFortress/` as the harness does, because an import is looked up in the current directory first:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress -debug stacktrace tests/X.fss

The direct run and the harness use different heaps (`interpreter.md`, "Running a program").

### Compiled tests

Compiled tests are the `.test` files in `compiler_tests/`, `library_tests/` and `other_compiler_tests/`. They link with the library's jars in the tree's `default_repository/caches`. If a build started the caches again, or the tree's caches are empty, run the library order first (`build-and-caches.md`). The tests of `one_library_tests/` compile against the one library, and a run test there needs the jars of its fourteen components. Run the tests in one of these ways:

- `ant testOneLibrary` compiles the fourteen first, with `OneLibraryComponents.test`, in its own caches folder, `ProjectFortress/test-caches/fast-onelibrary`. Each suite deletes that folder when it starts, and only `testFast` and `testOneLibrary` fill it again.
- With `junit.sh`, set `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one ONE_JVM=1`, and name `OneLibraryComponents.test` first. The compiles write to `default_repository/caches-one`, and the jars stay there after the call. Its `FortressLibrary` alone takes about 135 to 160 s, so run the call in the background (`session.md`).
- For a run by hand against the onelibrary track's jars, set `FORTRESS_CACHES=<tree>/ProjectFortress/test-caches/fast-onelibrary` and `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. The build does not touch that folder, so run `ant testOneLibrary` again after an edit of Java or Scala.

The script is `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh`. `climb-batch-N` is the folder's real name, not a placeholder. Run your own tree's copy: it runs the tree that it is in.

    ONE_JVM=1 explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh <label> \
        ProjectFortress/compiler_tests X.test Y.test > <tree>/tmp/junit-<label>.txt 2>&1

- `<label>` is any word. It marks the run's lines in the output. The script writes to standard output only, so redirect it to your `tmp/`.
- With `ONE_JVM=1`, the whole list runs in one `fortress junit` run, in one JVM. The compile and link tests run before the run tests, as in the suite. Without `ONE_JVM=1`, each file gets its own JVM.
- It removes the named components' entries from the tree's `default_repository/caches` before the whole list and after it, not between files. So a link test and the run test that uses its jar pass in one call, with or without `ONE_JVM=1`.
- It runs the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/` and builds nothing, as `harness-one.sh` does.
- It removes the Java stack frames, and cuts each line at 240 characters.
- Its JVMs keep their temporary files in the tree's `tmp/`, and run at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4`.

To run the same list in one JVM without the script, and without its removal of cache entries:

    cd ProjectFortress && ../bin/fortress junit compiler_tests/X.test compiler_tests/Y.test

Run all the new files of one test folder together, in one JVM, as the suite does. A test that passes alone can fail beside others.

## One unit-test class, or one track

To run one unit-test class: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=BitsJUTest`. It uses the tree's own caches and the shell's `FORTRESS_THREADS`.

To run tracks of testFast whole, run their target. Each target runs its tracks as testFast does, with the same JVMs and private caches:

- `ant testCompiler`: the compiler and othercompiler tracks.
- `ant testOtherCompiler`: the othercompiler track.
- `ant testLibrary`: the library track.
- `ant testQuick`: the three tracks.
- `ant testOneLibrary`: the onelibrary track.

# The base build, seeded worktrees and the old code

**seeding**
: Making a worktree with a copy of the build and caches of a built, clean worktree. `seed-worktree.sh` makes the copy and rewrites the paths in it (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").

**base build**
: Clean worktree at the base, built in place by ant, or seeded. Every other worktree is seeded from it.

**old code**
: Base's code, run from the base build with a private caches folder.

Once the base build is built, run its code only as "Running the old code" says, with a private caches folder outside it. Any other run writes into the caches that every worktree is seeded from.

## Finding or building a base build

- If your brief names a base build, use it.
- If not, look in `git worktree list`. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`. A worktree can be your base build if it passes three checks:
  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
- If no worktree passes them, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s: start the build and the library order detached, with the `nohup` line of `session.md`, "Long commands". `<base-commit>` is your base: the commit that your brief names, else your tree's `HEAD` when you start. Say so in your report.

      git worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
      ant compileAll
      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean

If you check a fix against its old code, use a base build at the commit that the fix starts from. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. If not, the fix starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`.

## Seeding a worktree

A build, and a run of `bin/fortress` without a private caches folder, walk's too, write into the caches of the tree that they run in. So build and run only in a tree whose caches no other agent uses. Your brief says where you work. If your work builds or runs code and your brief gives you no tree of your own, seed a worktree of your own instead of building one. Then work only there.

Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB of disk. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path right away, with the library already compiled.

    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]

- The script checks out `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>`, by default the base build's commit. With `-`, it makes a detached worktree at `<start-point>`.
- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.
- If the worktree already exists, the script keeps its branch. If it already has a build, the script keeps that too. `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces it.
- If you start in a worktree that has no build, seed it in place: name it as `<new-worktree>`, and its branch as `<branch>`.
- The script lists the library sources that differ from the base build's commit. Before a compiled run, take for each the step that `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library", gives.
- If the script warns that the copied build is the base's, run `ant compileAll`, then the library order. Without the warning, `ant compileAll` keeps the seeded caches.
- If another agent seeded your worktree, make the script's two lists yourself: `git diff --name-only <base> -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` for the library sources, and `git diff --name-only <base> -- ProjectFortress/src ProjectFortress/astgen build.xml` for the warning.
- Reuse another tree's build or caches only through this script.

## Running the old code

If your worktree holds an edit and you need the base's behaviour, run the old code instead of reverting your edit. For example, see a test fail, or compare a program's old and new output.

`old-fortress.sh` runs the base build's `bin/fortress`. It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private caches folder that you name, over your settings. Name a folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:

    OLD=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test [Y.test ...]   # compiled .test files, in one JVM

- Any copy of the tool works, because it runs the base build that its first argument names.
- On first use, it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). Later runs use the same folder.
- Every cache file that a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing else that it writes under the base build stays. So several agents can run the old code at once.
- Keep your programs outside the base build too, because a program writes its own logs beside it. The tool refuses a private folder inside the base build (exit 2).

To run interpreter tests on the old code, run the base build's `harness-one.sh` with `FORTRESS_HOME` set to the base build:

    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss

The `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process. It inherits `FORTRESS_HOME` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`, and takes its class path from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. If you compose a harness run by hand with `-Dfortress.caches=<folder>`, set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the same folder. Otherwise the `run` step fails with "Could not load ... Resource not found".

#!/bin/bash
# old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...
#
# Runs the old code, the base's: bin/fortress of the batch's one base build, with FORTRESS_HOME set to the
# base build and FORTRESS_CACHES to a private caches folder. If the folder does not exist yet, it is first
# made as a copy of the base build's default_repository/caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). The paths in those caches
# are the base build's own, so nothing is translated, and no worktree is made.
#
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss    the compiled path: compile ...
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P            ... then run
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss            walk
#
# Every cache a run writes goes to the private folder: every cache directory and the logs are under
# fortress.caches (repository/ProjectProperties.java:283-299), which FORTRESS_CACHES sets, and
# bin/fortress_classpath and bin/run_classpath put FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache on the class path.
# Under the base build a run reads the build, the library sources and default_repository/configuration, and
# writes nothing that stays: the parser writes its error logs beside each file it parses from source and
# deletes them (compiler/Parser.java:349-367), so a compile of a program that exports Executable creates and
# deletes two empty, gitignored logs beside Library/Executable.fsi. Two runs at once may share those two
# names; that is harmless, because the base's library parses without errors, so both logs stay empty and
# a log removed by the other run reads as empty (Parser.java:373-377). Measured in
# explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md, section 6.
#
# Keep the private folder and your programs outside the base build (the program's own logs go beside it).
# Refuses (exit 2) a base build that is not built, and a private folder inside the base build.
set -euo pipefail
USAGE='usage: old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...'
BASE=$(realpath "${1:?$USAGE}")
PRIV_ARG=${2:?$USAGE}
shift 2
[ -x "$BASE/bin/fortress" ] && [ -e "$BASE/ProjectFortress/build/com/sun/fortress/Shell.class" ] \
  && [ -e "$BASE/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar" ] \
  || { echo "old-fortress: $BASE is not a built tree" >&2 ; exit 2 ; }
PRIV=$(realpath -m "$PRIV_ARG")
case "$PRIV/" in "$BASE"/*) echo "old-fortress: $PRIV is inside the base build $BASE" >&2 ; exit 2 ;; esac
if [ ! -d "$PRIV" ]; then
    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$PRIV")"
    PART="$PRIV.part.$$"
    cp -a "$BASE/default_repository/caches" "$PART"
    mv -T "$PART" "$PRIV" 2>/dev/null || rm -rf "$PART"     # another run made it first: use that one
fi
FORTRESS_HOME="$BASE" FORTRESS_CACHES="$PRIV" exec "$BASE/bin/fortress" "$@"

simultaneously in a single atomic step with respect to \emph{any}
action performed by any thread which is dynamically outside.  This is
specified in detail in \chapref{memory-model}.  The value and type of an
\KWD{atomic} expression are the value and type of its body expression.

A \KWD{tryatomic} expression consists of \KWD{tryatomic} followed by
an expression.  It acts exactly like \KWD{atomic} except that in
certain circumstances (see \secref{transactions}) it throws
\TYP{TryAtomicFailure} and discards the effects of its body.

A function or method with the modifier \KWD{atomic} acts as if its entire
body were surrounded in an \KWD{atomic} expression.
However, it is a static error if an API declares a functional \VAR{f}
with the modifier \KWD{atomic} but a component implementing the API
defines \VAR{f} whose body is an \KWD{atomic} expression without the
modifier.  Functionals with the modifier \KWD{io} cannot be called
within an \KWD{atomic} expression.  Thus, a
functional must not have both \KWD{atomic} and \KWD{io} modifiers.

When the body of an \KWD{atomic} expression completes abruptly, the
\KWD{atomic} expression completes abruptly in the same way.  If it
completes abruptly by exiting to an enclosing \KWD{label} expression,
writes within the block are retained and become visible to other
====
(* An exception thrown out of a tryatomic block reaches the catch clause around it and discards the block's writes, as out of an atomic block. atomic.tex, section "Atomic Expressions". *)
component XXXThrowOutOfTryAtomicWalk
export Executable

object Boom extends UncheckedException end

var t: ZZ32 = 0

run(): () = do
  var caught: ZZ32 = 0
  try
    tryatomic do
      t := 3
      throw Boom
    end
  catch e
    Boom => caught := 1
  end
  assert(caught, 1, "an exception thrown out of a tryatomic block reaches the catch clause around it")
  assert(t, 0, "an exception thrown out of a tryatomic block discards the block's writes")
end

end
(* An exit out of a tryatomic block to an enclosing label reaches the label and keeps the block's writes, as out of an atomic block. atomic.tex, section "Atomic Expressions". *)
component XXXExitOutOfTryAtomicWalk
export Executable

var t: ZZ32 = 0

leave(): () = label done
    tryatomic do
      t := 3
      exit done
    end
  end done

run(): () = do
  leave()
  assert(t, 3, "an exit out of a tryatomic block reaches its label and keeps the block's writes")
end

end

writes within the block are retained and become visible to other
threads.  If it completes abruptly by throwing an uncaught exception,
all writes to objects allocated before the \KWD{atomic}
expression began evaluation are discarded.  Writes to newly
allocated objects are retained.  Any variable reverts to the value it
held before evaluation of the \KWD{atomic} expression began.  Thus, the
only values retained from the abruptly completed \KWD{atomic} expression
will be reachable from the exception object through a chain of newly
allocated objects.

Atomic expressions may be nested arbitrarily; the above semantics
imply that an inner \KWD{atomic} expression is atomic with respect to
evaluations which occur dynamically outside the inner \KWD{atomic}
expression but dynamically inside an enclosing \KWD{atomic}.

content.content:
3. Wrong as a ground for a revert. The rung's section says of its decisions, "None names the mechanism" (`CLIMB-BATCH-35.md:494`). A fork "chooses where the record leaves an implementation open" (`CLIMB-BATCH-35.md:442`). W2's purpose clause, that the right side runs once, still holds: each element of the tuple expression is evaluated once, in the one declaration that it initializes. Against W2's wording stand the specification and P-173, and the specification is the standard (POSITIONS.md, P-25). A revert would land the refusal above for every typed tuple binding of a numeral at a non-default type: `(u: NN32, r: RR32) = (5, 0.5)`, `(un, uq): (NN32, QQ) = (5, 0.1)`, `(en, em): NN32... = (7, 8)`, the `var` form and the field form. A program meets that form more often than any form that the fix leaves refused.

## What lands unrepaired

After the fix, a typed tuple binding stops at load where four things hold together:

- its right side is not a tuple expression of as many elements as names;
- an array literal is written inside that right side;
- the literal is bound to a name declared at an array type;
- the binding is a top-level variable or a field.

An example is `(arr, n): (ZZ32[2], ZZ32) = if flag then ([4 5], 6) else ([7 8], 9) end`.

The base ran it. On the base each name's initializer was the right side's own field at the name's declared type (`DesugarerVisitor.java:872-874` at `13f4fdea75`), and that cell built the literal (`LazilyEvaluatedCell.java:71-74`). The skeptic's correction says so in its message (`git show f39d01a66a`):

    NEW-W-2: under walk an array literal in a
    tuple bound at a tuple type is not built, for a variable on the base and now
    for a tuple binding over an if (tests/XXXTypedTupleArrayLiteralWalk).

SKEPTIC.md calls the failure new only "against the worker's head" ("Failure modes"). In fact it is new against the base too. It is walk's existing gap in typed tuples, row 1105, which the base shows for `t: (ZZ32[2], ZZ32) = ([1 2], 3)`. The fix now reaches the same gap from a tuple binding: walk reads that binding as the checker does, as a binding at the tuple type (`Decls.scala:280-300`). The branch records the gap. It has a row in record.md, the XXX test `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXTypedTupleArrayLiteralWalk.fss`, and a workaround: bind the array to a name of its own.

A second output changes. Where a typed tuple binding's right side is not a tuple expression and does not convert, the message names the temporary, 'Type mismatch binding (5,6) ... to *tuple_<span> (type (NN32,String))' (SKEPTIC.md, "Failure modes"). On the base it named the variable.

**Why not a repair round.** Each way that removes the residue edits a file outside the rung's section. The section's files are `Evaluator.java`, `DesugarerVisitor.java`, the tests and row 152. Each way also changes how every walk binding converts its value:

- (a) `Coercions.coerceTuple` builds an array literal at an array element type, as `LazilyEvaluatedCell.java:71-74` does through `LHSEvaluator.topLevelArray`. This also repairs row 1105's variable form.
- (b) The temporary keeps its value raw, and each name converts its own element. Walk's local tuple binding works this way already: `interpreter/evaluator/BuildLetEnvironments.java:103-118` evaluates the right side once and binds each element through `LHSEvaluator`. This way needs `LazilyEvaluatedCell.java:76` and the field initializer to skip `Numerals.plain` for the temporary: the skeptic's way (d).

The residue is narrow and recorded, and both ways stay open, so the rung lands now and the residue goes to the curator.

## Points this ruling adds

- A decision taken where nothing on record settles it: a narrow regression against the base lands, the `if` form above, rather than a repair beyond the rung's files. The ways are (a) and (b) above.
- Reserved point, an interpreter output that changed: the residue and the message above, beside those in REPORT.md, "Points to report", 6.

Neither is a step that cannot be undone, nor one against a decision on record. Neither holds the push.

tests=XXXOverrideConditionalExtensionChecker
typecheck
typecheck_err_contains=Invalid overloading of f in trait G
(* A generic trait that extends a trait under a where clause bounding its static parameter by ZZ32 overrides, with an override over ZZ32, the declaration it inherits there over that parameter, so the program type checks (traits.tex, sections "Traits" and "Method Declarations"). *)
component XXXOverrideConditionalExtensionChecker
export Executable

trait A[\T\]
  f(x: T): String = "A"
end

compile

FACTS.md:275
- F-363 **A superscript follows a dotted access and a parenthesised call on both paths.** `p.wq^T`, `B.n^2`, `B.f()^T` and `B.data[5]^2` parse as the operator applied to the whole dotted primary to its left, and `(f(x))^T`, `(f(x))!` and `(a^b)!` run under walk as they do compiled; `f(x)^T` and `f(x)^2` stay a static error on both paths (walk: "the argument should not be immediately followed by a non-expression element"; the checker: "Item at this location must be an expression, not an operator."). The parser reads a primary with a dot as the front of the math items that follow it (`parser/Expression.rats:386-400`), so a subscript, a parenthesised item or a tight identifier after a dotted method call parses too; of these, one test compiles a subscript, `Maker.f()[5]^2` (`compiler_tests/SubscriptThenSuperscriptCompiled`). The one node kind that the parser builds for a single item is the one the parenthesised spelling built, so neither the checker nor the code generator changed. Walk's postfix branch evaluates an operand in parentheses as one expression (`interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java:965-970`). So a model line may write `p.wq^T x` and `(onehot(ks, 5))^T dx`; a selector after a superscript, `B.data^T.v`, is still a syntax error, and a superscript after a subscript that is a math item of its own, `x[5]^2` or `B.f()[5]^2`, compiles (F-387) and runs under walk (F-398); in `B.data[5]^2` the subscript is part of the dotted primary. Tests: `tests/SuperscriptAfterDottedAccess.fss`, `tests/SuperscriptAfterParenthesisedCall.fss`, `tests/SuperscriptAfterCallRefused.fss` with its `.test`, and `compiler_tests/SuperscriptAfterDottedAccessCompiled.test`, `SuperscriptAfterParenthesisedCallCompiled.test`, `XXXSuperscriptAfterCallRefusedCompiled.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-superscript-after/REPORT.md`, "Each form on the base and after" and "The trees".

FACTS.md:278
- F-369 **A top-level tuple binding compiles: each name is a top-level variable of its element's type, and the right side is evaluated once, at the first read of any name.** The checker gives the tuple that it rebuilds from the checked elements their tuple type, from which each name's thunk reads its own (`scala_src/typechecker/impls/Decls.scala:272-277`); where only some names declare a type and the right side is no tuple expression of as many elements, it checks the right side again against each name's type (`Decls.scala:324-336`). The code generator keeps the right side's value in a hidden class `<Component>$tuple$<first name>` and gives each name its own class, whose initializer takes its element out by the tuple's typed getter (`compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:6908`); a wildcard binds nothing. Every compiled top-level variable is initialized at its first read, not at load as under walk, so a binding of wildcards alone never evaluates its right side (row 1011). So a model line of this form compiles as written, the model's lines 17 to 19 among them, and a name bound so is typed as a single binding's is: `explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss:72`, `beta1 m`, is a new checker site against the one library (F-58). Under walk the same right side runs once too: a tuple expression binds each name to its own element, and any other right side binds a temporary at the names' types (F-398). The checker checks a local tuple binding's declared names beside untyped names in the same way (row 1029, fixed; `compiler_tests/LocalTupleBindingMixedTypes`, `XXXLocalTupleBindingMixedRefused`), and a typed tuple binding over an `if` with tuple branches compiles (row 1031, fixed). Tests: `compiler_tests/TopLevelTupleBindingCompiled.test`, `TopLevelTupleBindingImport.test`, `TopLevelTupleBindingMixedTypes.test`, `XXXTopLevelTupleBindingType.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-tuple-binding/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "The binding as compiled".

FACTS.md:290
- F-387 **The compiled path compiles a primary whose math items all apply in turn to its front: `x[5]^2` is `(x[5])^2` and `g[1][2]` is `(g[1])[2]`; and a subscript as a math item before a tightly juxtaposed item: `x[5]k` is `(x[5]) k`.** The checker checks the one application that the reassociation leaves, at the expected type, and writes each subscript as a call of the subscript operator's method, as the desugaring before it writes every other subscript (`scala_src/typechecker/impls/Operators.scala`). Walk runs these forms too (F-398), so a program for both paths may write them unparenthesised. Test: `compiler_tests/SubscriptThenSuperscriptCompiled.test`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-checker-small-gaps/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why", item 2.

# Climb batch 35: the gather's record

Written at the gather stage of climb batch 35 (2026-11-23), the first of the two runs of `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-35.md`, a housekeeping batch: each rung fixes defects where walk and the compiled path behave differently or depart from the specification, each closing its ledger row, test first. All five rungs were approved and landed: R (a numeral with a radix point keeps its leading zeros in its digit count), W (walk's subscript before a superscript, and its tuple binding run once), S (the compiled dispatch method of a functional method whose self is not first), O (the modifier `override` compiled, and the checker's refusal of one that overrides nothing) and A (an exit out of an atomic block keeps the block's writes).

**Preconditions.** `git status --porcelain` printed nothing, and `13f4fdea75` is an ancestor of `HEAD` (`git merge-base --is-ancestor`, exit 0). The batch's commits start after `bbb4b540306628d185adf13edd6cffc4f2237411`, the `HEAD` the gather started from; the eight commits between the base and it are boot notes, the review queue's triage and a process review, which touch only `explorations/coordinator/` (`BOOT.md`, `HELD.md`, `INDEX.md`, `review-queue.md`, `process-engineering/queue-triage-2026-11-23.md`, `tools/record-landing/skill-task.md`) and `explorations/reviews/process-dead-ends-2026-11-23.md`, none a file of a rung. No earlier launch had worked this stage: `main` held no commit of the batch and `tmp/gather/` no file of it, so one launch worked it.

**Scratch.** The patches are `tmp/gather/<slug>.patch` in the main tree, each `git diff 13f4fdea7557b867c808d0c32af5dd2a03901f4b...<branch>`, applied on `main` with `git apply --3way --index`, each rung's record folded and its commit made. The branches are left as they were.

## The landed commits

| Rung | Slug | Branch head | Commit on `main` |
|---|---|---|---|
| R | `rung-radix-point-leading-zeros` | `5c2057ac57` | `6f0e48f187` |
| W | `rung-walk-subscript-tuple-binding` | `f13795e57b` | `f8b05668eb` |

Then `8dc97a08df`, "Close the rows climb batch 35 fixed", and this record's commit.

## The rungs applied, in order

R, W, S, O, A: the manifest's order, kept. No rung lands only with another (`landsOnlyWith` is empty in this batch). Of the files the rungs edit (`git diff 13f4fdea75...<branch>` per branch, read before anything was applied), one is shared: `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, by R and O. R's lowest edited line there is 5486 (`@@ -5486,3 +5486 @@`, in the effect of the entry "The numeral types, their conversion and their default") and O's is 6422 (`@@ -6422,2 +6422 @@`, in the effect of `\seclabel{revival-supported}`), so R goes before O, which is the manifest's order too. W and A were expected to meet in `Evaluator.java` and O and A in `CodeGen.java`; neither pair did: A edits `BaseTask.java` and `FortressTaskRunner.java` only, and no other file is shared. The rungs that share no file keep the manifest's order.

## Conflicts

None. Every hunk applied cleanly: `git apply --3way --index` printed 'Applied patch to ... cleanly.' for each file that `main` held, and the new files applied directly. S's patch printed 'warning: 1 line adds whitespace errors.', a trailing space in a blank line of `OverloadSet.java` as the branch holds it; nothing was changed for it. `main`'s commits since the base touch none of the rungs' files. After the five commits, each rung's applied files equal its branch's (`git diff --stat wip/<slug> HEAD -- <the rung's files>`) except for the gather's own edits listed below: the placeholders replaced, O's re-anchored citations, O's `changes.tex` edits beside R's, and the gather's correction of the same effect.

## The lines that another rung's hunks moved

- R's hunk in `Specification/appendices/changes.tex` removed two lines before O's, so O's edited line, "Nothing checks \KWD{io}, and nothing reads \KWD{atomic} on a function.", is at `:6420` on `main` after O's commit, where O's branch has it at `:6422`; the gather's correction (below) then put six lines before it, at `:6426` now. O's `REPORT.md` cited the line after the edit three times (its historical line, "The specification", and "Sentences of the specification made false"'s "After"); each is re-anchored by symbol, to the effect of `\seclabel{revival-supported}`. Its "before" citation, `changes.tex:6422-6423`, is of the base and stays; so does `SKEPTIC.md:18`'s, which names the lines that the rung edited on the base.
- No other rung's hunk moved a line that a record cites: W edits one line of `Evaluator.java` in place, and the other shared-looking files are edited by one rung each. O's insertion of 84 lines in `CodeGen.java` moved F-315's citation of the modifier guard, `CodeGen.java:3381-3383`, which the gather's rewrite of F-315 re-anchors to `:3462-3465`, `fnDeclCompilableModifiers`.

## The tests on the merged tree

The build and every run below are of the code of `e8b20935d5`, A's commit, on the main tree; the commits after it change no code. The machine: nproc 4, Intel Xeon at 2.30 GHz, JDK 25.0.4.1.

content.content:
FACTS.md:295
- F-399 **The dispatch method of a trait's or an object's functional method reads each argument at its own local, wherever self stands.** The method is an instance method of the receiver's class, self in local 0 and the other arguments after it in their order; `OverloadSet.argumentLocal`, overridden in `ForTraitOrObject`, gives an argument before self's place the local after its place, for the type tests and the casts alike (`compiler/OverloadSet.java:2357-2363`, `:2495-2508`, `:1538`, `:1876`). A call reaches the method where the declaration that the top-level dispatch of the name chooses has a more specific one below it in the type, as an inherited one does; a declaration of the type with none below it is called at its exact signature, its body. Not reached: a generic functional method overloaded beside a plain one, on which the code generator stops first (row 724), and a generic functional method with self not first, which dies at another site (row 594). So an object or trait may overload an inherited functional method with self anywhere. Tests: `compiler_tests/FunctionalMethodOverloadSelfLast`, `FunctionalMethodCoverSelfSecond`, `FunctionalMethodSelfSecondReceiverTested`, `FunctionalMethodMeetNarrowedSelfNotFirst`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-self-not-first-dispatch/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

FACTS.md:296
- F-400 **The code generator compiles the modifier `override` by the checker's table of what an override keeps from being inherited, and the checker refuses an `override` that overrides nothing.** A trait's or an object's class holds the override and, at each hidden declaration's JVM signature, a bridge that runs it; no method runs the hidden declaration, and a dispatch over the override and the declarations of its name that it does not override is still written (`scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1798-1812`, `overriddenNotProvided`; `compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:1224-1237`, `overrideBridges`; `:1476-1484`, `dumpOverloadedMethodChaining`). The checker refuses an `override` that appears in no overriding pair of `providedAndOverridden`, equal parameter types included, as the traits chapter and walk do: 'Invalid override of f in object B: ... has the modifier override and does not override any inherited declaration.' (`scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:424`, `:763-789`). Two forms stay code-generator walls, an override of or by a method with static parameters of its own, and one in a generic type whose parameter types name a static parameter (row 1106); the checker refuses an override under a conditional extension that walk runs (row 1107) and checks none in an object expression (row 1108); under walk an object's override hides every inherited declaration of its name (row 1109). So a program may write `override` on the compiled path wherever no static parameter is involved. Tests: `compiler_tests/OverrideModifierCodeGeneration`, `OverrideBridgesCompiled`, `XXXOverrideNothingCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-override-compiled/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

FACTS.md:297
- F-401 **An exit out of an `atomic` block commits the block's transaction and keeps its writes, on both paths.** Compiled, the block's handler `BaseTask.leaveTransaction` commits on a `LabelExit` as `endTransaction` does at a normal end (`runtimeSystem/BaseTask.java:303-309`); walk's `FortressTaskRunner.doItOnce` commits on a `LabelException` as at a normal end (`interpreter/evaluator/tasks/FortressTaskRunner.java:133-141`). A commit that fails runs the block again, as at a normal end, and an exception other than an exit still discards the writes. A nested block's commit hands its writes to the outer one, whose commit on the same exit stores them. Neither path tells an exit to an enclosing label from one to a completed label block, so the latter commits the blocks it passes too (row 1041). Under walk an exit or an exception out of a `tryatomic` block that no `atomic` block encloses is wrapped in a `RuntimeException` and reaches neither its label nor a `catch` (rows 1110 and 1111). So a program may exit out of an atomic block (`Specification/basic/expressions/atomic.tex:59-63`). Tests: `tests/ExitOutOfAtomicWalk.fss`, `compiler_tests/ExitOutOfAtomicCompiled`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-exit-out-of-atomic/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "The tests: failing on the base, passing after".

FACTS.md:279
- F-372 **The code generator writes each inherited method once into a trait's or an object's class, runs the declaration of the lowest type that declares it, and forwards to a body that an imported api's trait holds.** For the class of a trait or an object the code generator leaves out each declaration whose method a type strictly below the declaring type declares again at the same parameter types, self apart. A dispatch method's gathering still compares declarations as schemas over each trait's own bounds, not at the instance. So the choice is a relation between two declarations, not the order of the gathered methods, and the library's shape of P-47, `MAX` in `StandardMinMax`, `StandardTotalOrder` and a type below, does not stop a class at load (row 990, fixed). A method that an imported api's trait declares without `abstract` counts as a body in that trait's class, so a trait that is not first in an extends clause gives its body, plain, generic and functional methods alike (row 732, fixed). The batch's planner chose both readings as defaults, and the curator has not decided them; by the traits chapter's text, an object that reaches one method along two paths, one through a trait that declares it again, inherits both declarations, and the checker refuses that form where the traits are self-typed and generic (row 1037). A functional method with self not first is written once, not again beside the dispatch method of the same name (row 571, fixed), so such a class loads, and its dispatch method reads each argument at its own local (F-399). Tests: `compiler_tests/TraitOwnMethodBesideInheritedCompiled`, `ApiTraitMethodNotFirstCompiled`, `TraitMethodDiamondRedeclaredCompiled`, `FunctionalMethodMeetNarrowedSelfNotFirst`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-method-forwarders/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why".

FACTS.md:280
- F-373 **The compiled path runs `label` and `exit`: an exit is a thrown `LabelExit` that names one evaluation of its label block, and reaches it from a loop's body and from another task.** `CodeGen.forLabel` makes a new target for each evaluation of the block and takes, in a handler, the exits that name it; `CodeGen.forExit` throws `LabelExit.of(value, target)` (`runtimeSystem/LabelExit.java`). A function expression or a task whose body exits captures the target as it captures any immutable variable. A group of forked arms joins the arms that it forked before the exit passes it: at four threads every forked iteration of a parallel `for` runs to its end or to its own exit, and the label's value is the exit of the first arm in the arms' order; at one thread the iterations after the exit do not run. No `catch` clause takes an exit. An exit out of an `atomic` block commits the block's transaction (F-401). So the one library's `Indexed.indexOf` compiles in its own form (the test's `Holder.indexOf`), and row 81 is fixed. Three of the compiled answers were chosen as the path was built, and the curator has not decided them; walk answers each otherwise: which evaluation an exit leaves where the block is evaluated again inside itself, compiled the one in which the exit's function was made (row 1042); whether a `catch` of `Exception` takes an exit, compiled no (row 1040); and what an exit is after its label block has completed, compiled an uncaught `LabelExit` that ends the program (row 1041). Three limits stand, each with its test: a `finally` clause on the exit's way does not run (row 890); a label block as a call's later argument fails verification (row 322); a label block whose value joins a numeral with a number stops the code generator (row 340), though by P-50 the numeral takes the label's expected type; a program binds the numeral to a typed variable first. Test: `compiler_tests/LabelExitCompiled`, which fails with 'Can't compile Label' without `forLabel` and `forExit`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-label-exit/REPORT.md`, "What changed and why" and "Points to report reached".
